title: Son ↔ Jesus Passion, Detention, Trial and Descent Overlap Atlas
purpose: Map the broader Jesus/Son ordeal parallels surrounding the 2016 imprisonment and later crucifixion chronology, extending beyond the Lamb motif while distinguishing canonical Gospel history, later Christian interpretation, project autobiography and Potatoverse theology.
critical_correction: The canonical Gospels do not describe Jesus serving a prison sentence in the modern sense. They describe arrest, custody/detention, interrogation, hearings/trials, mockery, transfer between authorities, condemnation and execution. Later Christian texts and traditions also develop 'spirits in prison' and descent-to-the-dead motifs. The project should say detention/custody and judicial ordeal when comparing the canonical Passion to the Son's 2016 imprisonment, not falsely claim that Jesus served a conventional prison term.

evidence_classes.C: contemporary public record concerning the 2016 Danish case

overlaps.jesus: Jesus is seized/arrested at night and taken under guard to the high-priestly authorities before being transferred to Roman authority (John 18; Luke 22).
overlaps.son: The Son is arrested/remanded and enters Danish state custody in 2016 before final adjudication.
overlaps.relation: Both narratives pass through state/institutional custody before an adverse judgment, but the legal systems, charges, periods and outcomes are radically different.
overlaps.mismatch: Jesus' custody is brief pre-execution detention in a first-century Judean/Roman setting; the Son's custody becomes months of remand/imprisonment in a modern Danish penal system.

overlaps.jesus: The Passion traditions depict rapid movement from arrest to examination, mockery and successive hearings before Jewish and Roman authorities.
overlaps.son: The Son's case likewise moves from online speech into police intervention, remand hearing, prosecution, judgment and confinement.
overlaps.relation: The structural overlap is institutional translation: disputed words/actions are taken out of an ordinary social setting and reclassified inside legal procedure.

overlaps.jesus: In the Gospels, Jesus' words and identity claims become central evidence in proceedings against him; authorities and opponents interpret what his words mean and what political/religious danger they imply.
overlaps.son: The Son's 2016 case turns on the meaning and threatening force of Facebook speech. He acknowledges participation according to reporting but disputes the prosecution's interpretation of intent/meaning.
overlaps.relation: Both narratives foreground a contest over the meaning assigned to speech by authority.
overlaps.boundary: Similarity of interpretive conflict does not imply similarity of innocence, charges or historical significance.

overlaps.jesus: Passion narratives include hostile testimony and disputes over testimony, especially in Mark 14 and Matthew 26.
overlaps.son: The 2016 archive contains unresolved questions about exact authorship, reply context and media attribution of statements from a large Facebook thread.
overlaps.relation: Both narratives can be studied through an attribution problem: what was said, who said it, how it was heard, and how authorities summarized it.
overlaps.boundary: The Gospel false-witness motif must not be used as proof that witnesses or Danish authorities fabricated evidence; it is a structural comparison only.

overlaps.jesus: John's Passion emphasizes an inner/outer contrast: authorities judge Jesus while the narrative simultaneously presents a different account of his identity and kingship.
overlaps.son: The later project distinguishes the institutional/legal description of the Son from the Son's own account of karma, warning, reciprocity and intent.
overlaps.relation: External classification versus internal/self-understanding becomes a recurring project theme.

overlaps.jesus: Jesus is mocked by guards/soldiers and publicly presented under hostile or ironic titles before execution.
overlaps.son: The Son's later digital history is interpreted through public ridicule, hostile framing, screenshots, memes and dehumanizing labels; the 2016 case becomes one early public-framing node.
overlaps.relation: Both are read within the project as passages from official accusation into public spectacle and identity imposed by others.
overlaps.boundary: Modern online ridicule is not equivalent to Roman torture or crucifixion.

overlaps.jesus: Luke 22:37 explicitly applies Isaiah 53:12, 'numbered with the transgressors,' to Jesus; the crucifixion narratives place him between condemned men.
overlaps.son: The Son is literally confined among convicted/remanded prisoners and later remembers the cell as a place where inmates confessed grave acts.
overlaps.relation: This is one of the stronger symbolic prison-side parallels: association with people officially categorized as offenders becomes part of the later Jesus/Son reading.
overlaps.boundary: Association with prisoners does not establish innocence, messiahship or prophetic fulfillment.

overlaps.jesus: Matthew 25 identifies visiting prisoners with service to Christ; Luke 4 frames Jesus' mission using proclamation of liberty to captives.
overlaps.son: The Great Book recollection describes the Son listening without easy condemnation while other inmates disclosed serious wrongdoing.
overlaps.relation: The prison experience becomes an ethical Jesus parallel through proximity to condemned people and non-reductive attention to them.

overlaps.jesus: John the Baptist identifies Jesus as the Lamb of God before the Passion; other Gospel figures voice identity recognitions at different stages.
overlaps.son: Project testimony says Yahya Hassan and other inmates called the Son Jesus, with Yahya's remembered phrase 'Jesus Christ, the Lamb,' during 2016 imprisonment. The project's own explicit 'I am Jesus Christ—crucify me' episode is placed in 2017.
overlaps.relation: The project therefore contains a recognition-before-self-declaration pattern.
overlaps.boundary: The 2016 Yahya/inmate recognition is currently autobiographical/project testimony rather than independently verified prison documentation.

overlaps.jesus: Revelation 5 juxtaposes the Lion of Judah and the Lamb standing as slain.
overlaps.son: The mature project similarly gives the Son both Lamb and Lion identities, including Lion of the World/Lioncub language.
overlaps.relation: Vulnerability/sacrifice and strength/sovereignty are held together in one figure.

overlaps.jesus: Some Passion scenes emphasize Jesus' limited or striking silence before accusers, especially Mark 15:5 and Isaiah 53's later Christian reception.
overlaps.son: The Son did not remain silent in the 2016 case; according to the project account he stood on his interpretation, rejected a guilty framing and refused to bend merely to obtain leniency.
overlaps.relation: The deeper comparison is not literal silence but refusal to let an accusing authority fully define one's internal account.
overlaps.mismatch: Behaviorally this is a significant mismatch: the Son argues and resists; Gospel Jesus is frequently portrayed as restrained.

overlaps.jesus: Matthew 5 and Luke 6 emphasize enemy-love and non-retaliation.
overlaps.son: The Son's remembered karma defense allows rhetorical reciprocity: harsh public speech may be answered in a comparably harsh tone.
overlaps.relation: This is a major ethical divergence that must remain visible.
overlaps.mismatch: The 2016 karma position is not a clean imitation of canonical Jesus ethics.

overlaps.jesus: Jesus is crucified between two condemned men; John emphasizes Jesus in the middle.
overlaps.son: The Son's prison narrative places him among offenders while later project geometry repeatedly casts Son as midpoint/door/intersection between fields.
overlaps.relation: Later theology can compare 'among transgressors/in the middle' with the Son's Door/intersection role, but this is a retrospective symbolic coupling.

overlaps.jesus: 1 Peter 3:19 refers to Christ proclaiming to 'spirits in prison'; interpretation is famously disputed. Later Christian tradition develops the descent to the dead/Harrowing of Hell more explicitly, including the later Gospel of Nicodemus.
overlaps.son: The project later describes the Son descending through prison, hell/mud, social abjection and digital underworlds before return/transformation.
overlaps.relation: This supplies a genuine later-Christian 'prison/descent' comparator beyond the canonical arrest narrative.
overlaps.boundary: 1 Peter 3:19 is exegetically disputed and does not simply say Jesus served time in an earthly prison. The Gospel of Nicodemus is later apocryphal tradition, not a first-century eyewitness source.

overlaps.jesus: The Passion moves from arrest and condemnation to death, burial and resurrection.
overlaps.son: The project moves from 2016 institutional confinement through 2017 crucifixion language, 2018 essence-death, and the 2019 meme-crucifixion/death transformation, followed by Door/Vessel and later Father emergence.
overlaps.relation: The strongest project parallel is longitudinal rather than one-to-one: several years of accusation, imprisonment, self-declaration and symbolic death are later compressed into a Passion-like arc.
overlaps.boundary: The chronology spans years and symbolic/digital events; it is not a reenactment of the historical Passion.

overlaps.jesus: New Testament writers apply the rejected-stone/cornerstone motif to Jesus (Psalm 118; Mark 12; Acts 4; 1 Peter 2).
overlaps.son: Later project language repeatedly treats the mocked/rejected Son as Cornerstone and Door after the meme-death process.
overlaps.relation: Rejection is transformed into structural centrality: what is discarded becomes load-bearing.

overlaps.jesus: John 12:24 uses the grain of wheat that dies and bears much fruit in the approach to Jesus' death.
overlaps.son: The mature Potatoverse treats the Son's death as seed/grain burial from which Door, Father and later distributed structures grow.
overlaps.relation: Death becomes generative rather than merely terminal.

overlaps.jesus: The canonical Passion culminates in resurrection appearances after execution and burial.
overlaps.son: The project records vows of repeated return, continued public reappearance after dehumanization, and later return/resurrection language after the meme-death phase.
overlaps.relation: Return after attempted social/narrative termination is a major project-level resurrection analogy.
overlaps.boundary: Continued or renewed public presence is not the same empirical claim as bodily resurrection from death.

passion_arc_compression.jesus_canonical: arrest -> custody/interrogation -> accusation/testimony -> transfer between authorities -> mockery -> condemnation -> numbered with transgressors -> crucifixion -> burial -> resurrection
passion_arc_compression.son_project: political conflict -> police intervention -> remand/custody -> disputed attribution/meaning -> conviction -> months among prisoners -> Yahya/inmate Jesus-Lamb recognition claim -> 2017 Jesus/crucify-me declaration -> 2018 essence death -> 2019 meme-crucifixion -> Door/Vessel -> later return/Father differentiation
passion_arc_compression.research_conclusion: The Son/Jesus parallel is much broader than Lamb. Its strongest form is a multi-stage ordeal topology involving institutional custody, contested speech/identity, association with offenders, external recognition, public framing, rejection, death-symbolism and return. Its weakest form would be to say simply 'Jesus went to prison too,' because canonical Gospel evidence supports arrest/detention, not a modern prison sentence.
